::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 4 · Lesson 9 · About 75 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: a library card and the staff room"}
With a library card you can borrow books and see your own borrowing list, but not anyone else's. Some doors (the staff room) need a staff badge, and showing a library card there gets a polite "no".

Two separate checks are at work: *who* you are (your card) and *what that lets you do* (your list only; staff doors only with a badge). Atlas does the same with **ownership** (your saved issues, your notes) and **roles** (admins add repositories).
:::

## Theory

### Many-to-many, again

A user can save many issues, and an issue can be saved by many users: a **many-to-many** relationship. Lesson 3.4 modelled one already (issues and labels) with a **join table**: a table whose rows each link one of each. `saved_issues` has `(user_id, issue_id, saved_at)`, and its primary key is the pair, so the same issue can't be saved twice by the same user.

### Authorisation checks

After authentication (lesson 4.7) every request has a user. Authorisation decides what that user may do. Two common forms:

- **Role-based**: "only admins may add repositories". Check the user's role.
- **Ownership-based**: "you may edit only your own notes". Check the row's owner. The cleanest way is to put the owner into the query itself: `WHERE id = :note_id AND user_id = :me`. A row that isn't yours is simply not found.

### Which status code?

| Status | Meaning | Atlas example |
|---|---|---|
| **401 Unauthorized** | "Who are you?" No valid credentials. | no token on `PUT /issues/1/saved` |
| **403 Forbidden** | "I know who you are, and you may not." | a non-admin calls `POST /repos` |
| **404 Not Found** | It doesn't exist, *or* you mayn't know it exists. | someone else's note |

Why 404 for someone else's note rather than 403? A 403 confirms the note exists, which leaks information (that note ids are in use, how many there are). For private, per-user data, "not found" is the honest answer from your point of view. GitHub does the same for private repositories.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  Q[request] --> T{valid token?}
  T -->|no| U[401]
  T -->|yes| R{route needs admin?}
  R -->|yes, not admin| F[403]
  R -->|no, or admin| O{row belongs to user?}
  O -->|no| N[404]
  O -->|yes| OK[200 / 204]
```

### Idempotent saving with PUT

"Save issue 42" is naturally idempotent: saving it again should change nothing and still succeed. So it's `PUT /issues/42/saved`, and in SQL it's an insert that ignores conflicts: Postgres's `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. `DELETE /issues/42/saved` is idempotent too: deleting something already gone still leaves it gone. Both answer **204 No Content**: success, nothing to send back.

## In the project

The join table in `models.py`, written as a plain `Table` because it has no behaviour of its own:

```python
saved_issues = Table(
    "saved_issues",
    Base.metadata,
    Column("user_id", ForeignKey("users.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), primary_key=True),
    Column("issue_id", ForeignKey("issues.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), primary_key=True),
    Column("saved_at", DateTime(timezone=True), nullable=False, server_default=func.now()),
)
```

`ondelete="CASCADE"`: when a user or an issue is deleted, their saved rows go too (lesson 3.5).

### Saving and unsaving: `routes/issues.py`

```python
@router.put("/{issue_id}/saved", status_code=status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)
def save_issue(issue_id: int, user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> Response:
    """PUT is idempotent: saving an already-saved issue changes nothing and still succeeds."""
    get_issue_or_404(session, issue_id)
    session.execute(
        insert(saved_issues)
        .values(user_id=user.id, issue_id=issue_id)
        .on_conflict_do_nothing(index_elements=["user_id", "issue_id"])
    )
    session.commit()
    return Response(status_code=status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)
```

`insert` here comes from `sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql`, which adds `on_conflict_do_nothing`. `CurrentUser` makes the route require a login; `user.id` makes the row belong to whoever is signed in. There's no way to save an issue *for someone else*: the user id never comes from the request body.

```text
$ curl -s -X PUT http://localhost:8000/issues/1/saved -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -w "%{http_code}\n"
204
$ curl -s -X PUT http://localhost:8000/issues/1/saved -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -w "%{http_code}\n"
204
$ curl -s http://localhost:8000/users/me/saved-issues -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
[{"id":1,"repo":"pytorch/ignite","number":20,"title":"Support new metric","url":"https://github.com/pytorch/ignite/issues/20","author":"contributor","labels":["help wanted"],"comments":2,"created_at":"2026-11-02T09:14:00Z"}]
```

(`-w "%{http_code}\n"` makes curl print the status code.)

### Listing my saved issues: `routes/users.py`

```python
@router.get("/me/saved-issues", response_model=list[IssueOut])
def list_saved_issues(user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> list[IssueOut]:
    statement = (
        select(Issue)
        .join(saved_issues, saved_issues.c.issue_id == Issue.id)
        .where(saved_issues.c.user_id == user.id)
        .order_by(saved_issues.c.saved_at.desc())
        # Load every issue's labels and repo in one extra query each, not one per issue (N+1).
        .options(selectinload(Issue.labels), selectinload(Issue.repo))
    )
    return [issue_out(issue) for issue in session.scalars(statement)]
```

`saved_issues.c.user_id` is how you refer to a column of a plain `Table` (`c` for columns). `selectinload` is explained in lesson 4.10.

### Admin-only routes: a role dependency

In `deps.py`, a dependency built on top of `CurrentUser`:

```python
def require_admin(user: CurrentUser) -> User:
    is_admin = user.role == "admin"
    if not is_admin:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN, "Administrators only")
    return user


AdminUser = Annotated[User, Depends(require_admin)]
```

A route that takes `admin: AdminUser` is now admin-only, with no check inside the route. `routes/repos.py`:

```python
@router.get("", response_model=list[RepoOut])
def list_repos(session: SessionDep) -> list[Repo]:
    return list(session.scalars(select(Repo).order_by(Repo.full_name)))


@router.post("", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED, response_model=RepoOut)
def add_repo(body: RepoCreate, admin: AdminUser, session: SessionDep, ...) -> JSONResponse:
    exists = session.scalar(select(Repo.id).where(Repo.full_name == body.full_name)) is not None
    if exists:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_409_CONFLICT, f"{body.full_name} is already tracked")
    ...
```

(The full version also handles idempotency keys, lesson 4.12.) A regular user, then the same user after `atlas make-admin`:

```text
$ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/repos -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"full_name\": \"sktime/sktime\"}"
{"error":{"code":"forbidden","message":"Administrators only","request_id":"558237a62ed54108bcc617175fdc502d"}}

$ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/repos -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"full_name\": \"sktime/sktime\"}"
{"id":3,"full_name":"sktime/sktime","indexed_at":null}
```

Adding a repository only records it. Indexing it (downloading and chunking its files) is slow work for the background worker in Part 5.

## Common mistakes

- **Taking the user id from the request** (`{"user_id": 7, ...}`) instead of from the token. Anyone could act as anyone.
- **Checking ownership after loading**, in Python, in some routes and forgetting in others. Filter by owner in the query.
- **403 for private resources** that should be invisible: it confirms they exist.
- **401 when the user is known but not allowed**: that's 403.
- **Role checks copied into each route** instead of one `require_admin` dependency.
- **Check-then-insert for "save"**: a race. Let `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` decide.

## Check yourself

**1.** Why does `saved_issues` use `(user_id, issue_id)` as its primary key?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each pair can appear only once, so a user can't save the same issue twice, and the database enforces it. It also gives an index for "is this saved by this user?".
:::

**2.** A logged-in non-admin calls `POST /repos`. Which status, and why not 401?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
403 Forbidden. The user is authenticated (Atlas knows who they are), just not allowed. 401 would mean the credentials are missing or invalid.
:::

**3.** Why is "save" a PUT and not a POST?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Saving is idempotent: doing it twice has the same effect as once. PUT promises that; POST doesn't. Clients (and proxies) may safely retry a PUT.
:::

## Exercise

Write a test (or a curl session) showing that user B can't see user A's saved issues: A saves issue 1; B lists their saved issues.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
B's list is `[]`. The query filters by `saved_issues.c.user_id == user.id`, and `user` comes from B's token. The reference test `test_saving_is_idempotent_and_private` (lesson 4.15) does exactly this.
:::

## Stretch

Add `GET /issues/{issue_id}/saved` that answers `{"saved": true}` or `{"saved": false}` for the signed-in user, in one query.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
from sqlalchemy import exists


@router.get("/{issue_id}/saved")
def is_saved(issue_id: int, user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> dict[str, bool]:
    statement = select(
        exists().where(saved_issues.c.user_id == user.id, saved_issues.c.issue_id == issue_id)
    )
    return {"saved": bool(session.scalar(statement))}
```
`EXISTS` stops at the first match. Not in the reference code.
:::

## What changed in the project

`saved_issues` table; `require_admin` and `AdminUser` in `deps.py`; routes `PUT`/`DELETE /issues/{id}/saved`, `GET /users/me/saved-issues`, `GET`/`POST /repos`. Commit: `feat: Added saved issues and admin-only repositories`.
